summary: Defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module for managing DS0 and DS0 bundle interfaces, the basic digital voice-grade channels used in telephone-style circuits. It lets network management tools using SNMP monitor and configure them. It is a companion to the MIB documents for DS1/E1 and DS3/E3 interfaces.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2494 adds SNMP objects for the telephone interfaces that the standard Interfaces MIB does not cover. A DS0 is a small digital channel inside a bigger DS1 or E1 circuit, and a DS0 bundle is a group of those channels working together. The memo describes how to read and change each channel's settings, how to create a bundle, and how to map a channel number to the interface that carries it.

subtitle: SNMP management objects for DS0 channels and the bundles of DS0s that carry faster data inside a DS1 or E1.

tldr.problem: A router that carries telephone traffic exposes its interface configuration through SNMP, but the standard Interfaces MIB does not describe the small voice channels a DS1 or E1 circuit is divided into, nor the groups of those channels that are used together.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines two MIB modules, DS0-MIB and DS0BUNDLE-MIB. One describes a single DS0: its channel number, its signalling settings and the codes it puts on the wire. The other describes a bundle: how it is created, which DS0s belong to it, and which bonding mode it uses.
tldr.outcome: The modules sit at the roots 81 and 82 of the transmission branch of the MIB tree, and they are companions to the modules for DS1, E1, DS3 and E3 interfaces. The memo is explicit that writing the wrong value to several of the objects can cause loss of traffic, so it names them and recommends SNMPv3 access control.

facts.label: ABCD code bitmap
facts.value: 1 D bit, 2 C bit, 4 B bit, 8 A bit

today: RFC 2494 is an Internet standards track document at the Proposed Standard level, and it has not been obsoleted. It is a companion to the MIB modules for the DS1, E1, DS2, E2, DS3 and E3 interface types, and it was produced by the IETF Trunk MIB Working Group.

sections.title: The SNMP Management Framework
sections.content:
RFC 2494 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for use with network management protocols, in particular the objects used for managing DS0 and DS0 Bundle interfaces. It is a companion document to the MIB definitions for the DS1, E1, DS2 and E2 interface types in RFC 2495, for DS3 and E3 in RFC 2496, and to the work in progress on the SONET and SDH interface types.

A MIB is a virtual information store. The objects in it are accessed through the operations of a network management protocol, and they are described using the Structure of Management Information (SMI). The memo sets out the SNMP management framework as five parts: an overall architecture, described in RFC 2271; the mechanisms for describing and naming objects and events, the first version of the SMI being SMIv1 in RFC 1155, RFC 1212 and RFC 1215, and the second, SMIv2, in RFC 1902, RFC 1903 and RFC 1904; the message protocols for carrying management information, SNMPv1 in RFC 1157, SNMPv2c in RFC 1901 and RFC 1906, and SNMPv3 in RFC 1906 and RFC 2274; the protocol operations for accessing management information, in RFC 1157 and then RFC 1905; and a set of fundamental applications, in RFC 2273, together with the view-based access control mechanism of RFC 2275.

The memo's own module is written to be compliant with SMIv2. A module conforming to SMIv1 can be produced by translation, and the translated MIB must be semantically equivalent, except where an object or event has to be left out because no translation is possible, which the memo notes is the case for Counter64. Some machine readable information in SMIv2 becomes a textual description in SMIv1, and the memo does not consider that loss to change the semantics of the MIB.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is the catalogue of things a management system can read or change about a device. The memo describes where this catalogue fits in the SNMP framework and notes that the module is written in the second version of the notation, with an equivalent older version obtainable by translation.

sections.title: The Interfaces Described Here
sections.content:
These objects are used when the media used to realize an interface is a DS0 interface. At present that means two values of the ifType variable in the Internet-standard MIB: ds0 (81) and ds0Bundle (82).

A DS0 is the small digital channel that a DS1 or E1 circuit is divided into. A DS0 bundle is a set of DS0s used together to carry data inside a DS1 or E1 at a speed greater than a single DS0 can manage. The memo takes the terms that describe bonding modes from the BONDing specification, version 1.0 of the BONDING Consortium, and refers implementors there for the definitions.

Most of what a manager needs to know about a DS0 is already in the Interfaces Group MIB of RFC 2233, where only the ifGeneralInformationGroup and the ifCounterDiscontinuityGroup have to be supported. The memo fixes what the DS0 layer uses for the objects in that group. ifIndex is the interface index. ifType is ds0 (81) or ds0Bundle (82). ifSpeed is 64000 for a ds0, regardless of the setting of robbed bit signalling, or N*64000 for a ds0Bundle. ifPhysAddress holds the circuit identifier, or an octet string of zero length if no circuit identifier has been assigned. ifHighSpeed is the rounded ifSpeed divided by 1000000. ifLinkUpDownTrapEnable is set to disabled(2) and supports read-only access, and ifConnectorPresent is set to false(2). The remaining objects, including ifDescr, ifAdminStatus, ifOperStatus, ifLastChange and ifName, are used as the interfaces MIB defines them.
sections.plainLanguage: The objects apply to interfaces of type ds0 or ds0Bundle. A DS0 is a 64 kbit/s voice channel, and a bundle is a group of them working together. Most of the interface information comes from the standard Interfaces MIB, and the memo only fixes the values that differ for these two types.

sections.title: Stacking, Channelization and Index Mapping
sections.content:
The memo works through examples of how the standard ifStackTable shows the relationship between DS0 and bundle interfaces and the interfaces built on top of them. The examples are for illustration only, and an implementor of the stack table for these interfaces should look at the RFC for the service being stacked on them.

The first example carries a Frame Relay service on four DS0s of a DS1. A bundle of four DS0s sits between the service and the DS1. The ifIndex values could be 1 for the Frame Relay service, 2 for the bundle, 3 to 6 for the four DS0s and 7 for the DS1, and the stack table then shows the service above the bundle, the bundle above each of the four DS0s, and each DS0 above the DS1. When the Frame Relay service uses a single DS0 the bundle is not needed at all, and the stack table has only four entries.

The second example is channelization. A DS3 with ifIndex 1 channelized into DS1s sets the object dsx3Channelization to enabledDs1, which gives 28 DS1s in the ifTable, with ifIndex values 2 through 29 if the entries are created in channel order. The DS1 MIB then has one row in its dsx1ChanMappingTable for each DS1, mapping the DS1 ifIndex and the DS1 channel number to the ifIndex of that DS1. If the DS1s are then channelized into DS0s, dsx1Channelization is set to enabledDs0 and the agent creates 24 DS0s for that DS1; setting it to disabled destroys them again. With the DS0s of the first DS1 at ifIndex 30 through 53, the DS0 MIB has one row in dsx0ChanMappingTable for each DS0, mapping the DS1 ifIndex and the DS0 channel number to the DS0 ifIndex. Timeslot 16 is not created for framing types that do not pass data over it, and the treatment of E1 and E3 is similar with a different number of DS0s.

The third example shows the ifIndex mapping for a bundle. A DS1 with ifIndex 1 channelized into DS0s gives 24 DS0s, with ifIndex values 2 through 25. If the DS1 carries two bundles, the first using channels 1 and 2 and the second using channels 3 and 4, the two bundles take ifIndex values 26 and 27, and the dsx0BundleTable has one row for each. The dsx0ConfigTable then shows which bundle each DS0 belongs to, and a DS0 that belongs to no bundle has a mapped ifIndex of zero.
sections.plainLanguage: Three worked examples show how the interfaces fit together. A service such as Frame Relay can sit on a bundle of four DS0s, which sit inside a DS1. Channelizing a big interface into smaller ones is recorded in a mapping table, so a manager can go from a channel number to the interface that carries it. A third example shows which DS0s belong to which bundle.

sections.title: The DS0 Config Group
sections.content:
The DS0 MIB represents individual DS0s inside a DS1 or E1, with variables created for each DS0 in the ifTable. It holds a single group, the DS0 Config Group, whose implementation is mandatory for every system that uses a DS0 interface. The group has two tables.

The DS0 Configuration Table has one row for each DS0 interface, indexed by ifIndex. Its columns are dsx0Ds0ChannelNumber, the channel number of the DS0 on its DS1 or E1, a read-only integer from 0 to 31; dsx0RobbedBitSignalling, whether robbed bit signalling is on, which applies only to DS0s on a DS1 link and is always off for E1 links; dsx0CircuitIdentifier, the transmission vendor's circuit identifier kept to help with troubleshooting, a string of up to 255 characters; dsx0IdleCode, the code transmitted in the ABCD bits when the DS0 is not connected; dsx0SeizedCode, the code transmitted in the ABCD bits when it is connected; dsx0ReceivedCode, the code being received in the ABCD bits; dsx0TransmitCodesEnable, which decides whether the idle and seized codes are transmitted at all; and dsx0Ds0BundleMappedIfIndex, the ifIndex of the bundle the DS0 may belong to, or zero if it belongs to none.

The three code objects are bitmaps with the same bit positions: 1 for the D bit, 2 for the C bit, 4 for the B bit and 8 for the A bit, and each object has the range 0 to 15.

The DS0 Channel Mapping Table maps a DS0 channel number on a channelized interface to the ifIndex of the individual DS0. It is indexed by the ifIndex of the channelized interface together with the DS0 channel number, and its one column, dsx0ChanMappedIfIndex, holds the ifIndex of the DS0 ifEntry. The memo explains why the table is worth having: it gives the same information as the ifStackTable and the DS0 Configuration Table, but with a single table lookup instead of a walk through the stack table to find the constituent entries.
sections.plainLanguage: The main table has one row per DS0 channel. It records which channel number the DS0 is, whether robbed bit signalling is on, the vendor's circuit identifier, the codes the device puts on the wire when the channel is idle and when it is seized, the code currently arriving, and which bundle the channel belongs to. A second table turns a channel number into an interface index in one lookup.

sections.title: The DS0 Bundle and Bonding Groups
sections.content:
The DS0Bundle MIB represents collections of DS0s used together to carry data within a DS1 or E1 at speeds greater than a single DS0, and bundles are created on top of DS0s and represented that way in the ifStackTable. It has two groups. The DS0 Bundle Group holds the objects used for creating new bundles and is mandatory. The DS0 Bonding Group holds information about the bonding of a bundle when bonding is enabled and is optional.

The bundle group starts with dsx0BundleNextIndex, an object of the TestAndIncr syntax that helps the manager choose a value for dsx0BundleIndex. Because of that syntax it also lets several managers avoid racing each other when they create rows in the table. The algorithm the memo gives is: read the object, write the same value back, and if that write fails another manager has taken the value, so read a new one; then create the row with createAndGo.

The DS0 Bundle Table has a row for each bundle in the system and can be used indirectly to create rows in the ifTable with ifType of ds0Bundle(82). It is indexed by dsx0BundleIndex, a unique identifier for the bundle that is not the same value as an ifIndex, because the manager has to choose the index in a createable row while the agent must be allowed to select the ifIndex values. The remaining columns are dsx0BundleIfIndex, the ifIndex the agent selected for the new interface; dsx0BundleCircuitIdentifier, the vendor's circuit identifier for troubleshooting; and dsx0BundleRowStatus, used to create and delete rows.

The optional DS0 Bonding Table has a row for each bundle interface, indexed by ifIndex. dsx0BondMode says which bonding mode is used for the bundle, if any: none(1) when the interface is not performing bandwidth-on-demand, other(2), and mode0(3) through mode3(6). Mode 0 provides parameter and number exchange with no synchronization. Mode 1 provides parameter and number exchange, and also synchronization during initialization, but no inband monitoring. Mode 2 provides all of that plus inband monitoring, and also steals 1/64th of the bandwidth of each channel, so it does not support n x 56/64 kbit/s data channels for most values of n. Mode 3 provides all of the above and does support n x 56/64 kbit/s data channels, and most common implementations of Mode 3 add an extra channel to carry the inband monitoring overhead.

dsx0BondStatus gives the current status of the bonding call using the bundle: idle(1), callSetup(2) or dataTransfer(3), with idle(1) used when the bonding mode is set to none(1). dsx0BondRowStatus creates new rows in the table, modifies existing ones and deletes them.
sections.plainLanguage: The bundle module lets a manager build a group of DS0s and put a service on top of it. The manager picks a bundle number, the agent assigns the interface index, and a bonding mode records how the channels of the bundle behave towards each other. Mode 3 is the fullest: it keeps the full data rate of every channel at the cost of one extra channel for monitoring.

sections.title: Conformance and Compliance
sections.content:
Each module closes with its conformance information. In the DS0 MIB, ds0Compliance is the compliance statement for DS0 interfaces, and it makes the ds0ConfigGroup a mandatory group. The memo then lists the objects an implementation need not be able to write: dsx0RobbedBitSignalling, dsx0CircuitIdentifier, dsx0IdleCode, dsx0SeizedCode and dsx0TransmitCodesEnable may all be read-only, because the ability to set them is not required. The ds0ConfigGroup object group gathers the nine objects that provide configuration information applicable to all DS0 interfaces.

In the DS0Bundle MIB, dsx0BundleConfigGroup is mandatory and dsx0BondingGroup is optional. Two objects in the bundle table get a minimum access level. dsx0BundleRowStatus need only be read-only, and the agent is not required to support a SET on it, with only three of the six RowStatus values needing support: active(1), createAndGo(4) and destroy(6). Supporting only createAndGo for the creation process is what stops a manager creating an inactive row, and the memo says inactive rows in that table do not make sense. dsx0BundleCircuitIdentifier also only has to be read-only.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo says which parts a device must implement and which it may leave out. The DS0 configuration objects are mandatory but most of them only have to be readable, not writable. A bundle device must support creating bundles, while the bonding objects are optional.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo starts from the fact that SNMPv1 by itself is an insecure environment, and adds that even when the network itself is secure, for instance through the use of IPsec, there is still no control over who on that network is allowed to read the objects in this MIB. It recommends the security features of the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model of RFC 2274 and the View-based Access Control Model of RFC 2275.

It then places the remaining duty on the operator: the SNMP entity that gives access to an instance of this MIB has to be configured so that it grants access to these objects only to the principals, meaning users, that have a legitimate right to them.

The memo separates the objects by what happens when they are set to an inappropriate value. Setting dsx0RobbedBitSignalling, dsx0IdleCode, dsx0SeizedCode, dsx0TransmitCodesEnable, dsx0BundleRowStatus, dsx0BondMode or dsx0BondRowStatus wrongly can cause loss of traffic, and in the case of robbed bit signalling it changes the nature of the traffic flowing on the DS0. Setting dsx0CircuitIdentifier or dsx0BundleNextIndex wrongly is mischievous, but does no harm to traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo warns that these objects can stop traffic: turning on the wrong signalling setting or picking a bad bonding mode can cut calls. It also says the objects hold nothing secret, but that access to them should still be limited, and recommends the access control model of SNMPv3.

items.label: D bit
items.desc: Bit position 1 in the idle, seized and received code bitmaps.

items.desc: Bit position 2 in the idle, seized and received code bitmaps.

items.label: B bit
items.desc: Bit position 4 in the idle, seized and received code bitmaps.

items.label: A bit
items.desc: Bit position 8 in the idle, seized and received code bitmaps.

items.label: No bonding
items.desc: The interface is not performing bandwidth-on-demand.

items.label: Other
items.desc: A bonding mode not covered by the modes listed here.

items.label: Mode 0
items.desc: Parameter and number exchange, with no synchronization.

items.label: Mode 1
items.desc: Parameter and number exchange, plus synchronization during initialization, without inband monitoring.

items.label: Mode 2
items.desc: All of mode 1 plus inband monitoring, taking 1/64th of the bandwidth of each channel.

items.label: Mode 3
items.desc: All of mode 2, and n x 56/64 kbit/s data channels. Implementations usually add a channel for the monitoring overhead.

items.label: Bond status idle
items.desc: No bonding call in progress. Used when the mode is none(1).

items.label: Bond status call setup
items.desc: The bonding call is being set up.

items.label: Bond status data transfer
items.desc: The bonding call is carrying data.
